cent.900.smell: Kiev smelled of furs, beeswax and honey stacked for the river convoys to Constantinople.
cent.900.trouble: Old gods or new: Vladimir’s baptism of Kiev meets its fiercest resistance in the northern towns of Novgorod, Suzdal and Belozersk.
cent.900.powers.0.t: the caliphs under Turkish guards; Samanids in Bukhara
cent.900.powers.4.t: the Tang fell in 907; the Song from 960
cent.900.powers.5.t: gold and salt across the Sahara
cent.1000.moved: Leif Erikson settles briefly in Newfoundland about 1001; Ghaznavid raids open India to Islam; Rome and Constantinople divide in 1054; the Normans take England in 1066.
cent.1000.art: The great Chola bronzes and the Brihadisvara temple; Song landscape painting under Fan Kuan; Murasaki's Genji at the Heian court; Byzantine mosaics at Hosios Loukas.
cent.1000.life: Song China counts 20 million households, perhaps 90 million people. Its furnaces make more than 100,000 tonnes of iron a year, now on coal instead of charcoal; its mints strike some six billion copper coins in 1085, and the state prints the first government paper money. From 1011 a drought-proof rice from Champa gives two harvests a year. On the Mississippi, Cahokia rises about 1050 round a plaza of 50 acres. In Egypt the Nile fails, and Fustat empties in seven years of famine.
cent.1000.food: Rice in the south, two crops a year from Champa seed, with pork and salted fish for the poor; in Cairo in the famine of 1064 to 1071, dogs sold for five silver dirhams each until there were none left.
cent.1000.smell: Kaifeng smelled of coal, which the iron works now burned instead of charcoal, and of restaurants serving southern food to officials far from home.
cent.1000.trouble: Who rises and who starves: some 30,000 candidates a year sit the Song prefectural examinations, while in Egypt rival slave regiments of Turks and Sudanese fight over a weak caliph as some 40,000 people die of hunger.
cent.1000.powers.0.t: the richest state on earth; paper money and printing
cent.1000.powers.1.t: Basil II at the height of the recovery
cent.1000.powers.2.t: Shia caliphs rule Egypt and Syria
cent.1000.powers.5.t: Tamil sea power across the Bay of Bengal
cent.1100.moved: Crusaders sail from Genoa and Venice to the Levant; Arabic learning is translated at Toledo; the compass and gunpowder are in use in Song China.
cent.1100.art: Angkor Wat; the Romanesque pilgrimage churches of Vézelay and Santiago; Chartres rebuilt after 1194; Hildegard's chants; Song celadon.
cent.1100.life: In 1127 the Jurchen take Kaifeng with two emperors and most of the court, and the Song rebuild south of the Yangtze at Hangzhou, which grows from about 200,000 people to 500,000 by 1170; its paper-money works employ more than a thousand people a day. On the Mississippi, Cahokia is at its height, 15,000 or more in pole-and-thatch houses round Monks Mound, thirty metres of heaped earth; about 1175 it builds a palisade three kilometres long. By 1200 Kiev is about the size of Paris, and London has some 30,000.
cent.1100.food: In Hangzhou, breakfast sellers on the Imperial Way offer tripe, mutton, goose, soups and pancakes, and the noodle shops never close; at Cahokia, maize alongside the old seed crops, goosefoot and sumpweed.
cent.1100.smell: Hangzhou smelled of noodle shops open day and night and of night markets that shut at the third watch and opened again at the fifth; Cahokia, of thatch, wood smoke and the earth heaped onto its mounds.
cent.1100.trouble: Walls and war: the Song fight the Jurchen for the north, and Cahokia, once open, shuts itself behind a palisade that it rebuilds smaller and smaller as people leave.
cent.1100.powers.0.t: Huizong the painter-emperor; Kaifeng lost to the Jin in 1127
cent.1100.powers.1.t: Jerusalem taken in 1099; Saladin retakes it in 1187
cent.1100.powers.2.t: Turkish masters of Iran and Anatolia after Manzikert 1071
cent.1100.powers.3.t: the Investiture quarrel with the popes
cent.1100.powers.4.t: Berber rule from the Senegal to Spain
cent.1200.moved: Mongol horsemen ride from the Pacific to Hungary; Marco Polo travels the open roads to China; the Fourth Crusade sacks Constantinople in 1204.
cent.1200.art: The Gothic cathedrals of Chartres, Reims and Amiens; the Bayon at Angkor; Rumi at Konya; Persian miniature painting begins; Nicola Pisano at Pisa.
cent.1200.life: From 1206 the Mongols of Genghis Khan ride out, each soldier with five or six horses, sparing the cities that surrender and massacring those that resist, all but the craftsmen. Kiev falls in 1240, and Baghdad is sacked in 1258. Then comes a hard peace: merchants with papers travel under protection, and under Kublai some 1,400 relay stations with 50,000 horses carry messages 200 kilometres a day. Hangzhou passes a million people, and 400,000 candidates a year sit the Song examinations.
cent.1200.food: In Hangzhou the poor ate rice, pork and salted fish and the rich deer, hare, pheasant, quail and shellfish, rice wine was commoner than grape, and eleven kinds of apricot and eight of pear came to market.
cent.1200.smell: A Mongol relay station smelled of horses, oxen and mules by the thousand, kept ready every forty kilometres along the roads of the empire.
cent.1200.trouble: Conquest and tolerance: the Mongols massacre whole cities, yet decree freedom of religion, spare the poor and the clergy from tax and, from 1252, count every subject for a fixed poll tax.
cent.1200.powers.0.t: Genghis Khan proclaimed in 1206; Baghdad falls in 1258
cent.1200.powers.1.t: the richest city on earth until 1279
cent.1200.powers.2.t: Turkish sultans in north India from 1206
cent.1200.powers.5.t: Magna Carta 1215; Philip Augustus takes Normandy
cent.1200.powers.6.t: Sundiata's empire of the gold trade
cent.1300.moved: The Black Death moves from Caffa to Messina in 1347 and across Europe to Russia by 1351; Ibn Battuta travels from Tangier to China; Timur rises at Samarkand in 1370.
cent.1300.art: Giotto at Padua and Florence; Dante writing the Comedy; the Alhambra at Granada; the Sienese painters; Timbuktu's mosques about 1327.
cent.1300.life: Between 1346 and 1353 plague runs from the Crimea through Constantinople and Sicily to every corner of Europe and the Middle East, killing perhaps 30 to 60 per cent of Europeans and a third of the people of the Middle East. Half of Paris dies; Florence falls from some 120,000 people to 50,000; Cairo, with up to 600,000, loses more than a third in eight months. Earlier, in 1324, Mansa Musa of Mali had crossed Cairo on his way to Mecca with, later chroniclers said, eighty camels carrying gold.
cent.1300.food: In Yuan China Hu Sihui compiles the Yinshan Zhengyao, a guide to food and health that joins Mongol and Chinese cooking, and sorghum arrives from the west; in Mali the kings grow rich taxing the trade in salt and gold.
cent.1300.smell: Europe smelled of the plague pits, dug because there were too many dead for the churchyards, some holding hundreds or thousands of bodies; the doctors of Paris blamed a pestilence in the air.
cent.1300.trouble: Whom to blame: Jewish communities are attacked and destroyed, lepers too, while Ragusa invents quarantine in 1377 and wages, rents and taxes are thrown into disorder.
cent.1300.powers.1.t: Mongol successor states in Persia and the steppe
cent.1300.powers.2.t: the last crusader ports taken in 1291
cent.1300.powers.4.t: Philip the Fair; the Hundred Years' War from 1337
cent.1300.powers.5.t: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324
cent.1400.moved: Chinese fleets reach Malindi; Portuguese caravels work down the African coast; Gutenberg prints at Mainz; Constantinople falls in 1453; Columbus sails in 1492.
cent.1400.art: Early Renaissance Florence: Brunelleschi's dome, Donatello, Masaccio; the Van Eycks in Bruges; the Forbidden City; Timurid Samarkand and Herat; Inca stonework at Cuzco.
cent.1400.life: Tenochtitlan, on its island in Lake Texcoco, holds more than 200,000 people in four quarters of twenty districts each; commoners live in reed houses plastered with mud, most people bathe twice a day, and 20,000 or more trade daily at the Tlatelolco market. In the Andes the Inca, from 1438, rule perhaps ten million people without money or markets: each household owes the state labour, and storehouses stand a day’s walk apart. In Mainz, about 1440, Gutenberg begins to print; by 1500 Europe’s presses have made 20 million copies.
cent.1400.food: Potatoes of more than 200 kinds and chuño, potato freeze-dried, with maize beer, and coca leaves to ease hunger at work in the Andes; in Tenochtitlan, the harvest of the chinampa fields built out into the lake.
cent.1400.smell: Tenochtitlan smelled of its canals and canoes and of the spring water carried in from Chapultepec by two terracotta aqueducts; Constantinople in 1453 smelled of the powder of Orban’s great bombard.
cent.1400.trouble: Empire and faith: the Ottomans take Constantinople in 1453 with 50,000 to 80,000 men against 7,000 defenders and enslave perhaps 30,000 of its people, while the Inca move whole colonies of subjects across the Andes.
cent.1400.powers.0.t: Zheng He's fleets sail from 1405; the Forbidden City in the 1420s
cent.1400.powers.1.t: Timur captures Bayezid at Ankara in 1402
cent.1400.powers.5.t: expanding under Pachacuti; Machu Picchu about 1450
cent.1500.moved: Pepper reaches Lisbon round the Cape from 1499; Magellan's fleet circles the globe in 1519–1522; Cortés takes Tenochtitlan in 1521; silver begins to flow from Potosí.
cent.1500.art: The High Renaissance in Florence and Rome; the Northern Renaissance in Bruges and Nuremberg; Ming blue-and-white for the Indian Ocean trade; Sinan's mosques at Istanbul; Persian miniatures at Tabriz.
cent.1500.life: The oceans join the world, and the Americas pay. Smallpox appears there in 1518; in 1520 it kills perhaps 40 per cent of Tenochtitlan’s 200,000 people, and over the century Mexico falls from an estimated 20 million to barely more than one. At Potosí, founded in 1545 on a mountain of silver, Spain drafts some 13,000 Andean men a year into mines that yield 60 per cent of the world’s silver. In Germany, printers sell 300,000 copies of Luther’s writings between 1518 and 1520.
cent.1500.food: New crops cross the oceans: maize and sweet potatoes to China, where the sweet potato, arriving about 1560, becomes the food of the poor, cassava to Africa and tomatoes to Spain, while wheat, sugar cane, cattle, pigs and horses go west.
cent.1500.smell: Potosí smelled of mercury, used from 1554 to draw the silver out of the ore, and of the coca leaves that women sold in its street markets.
cent.1500.trouble: Who owns the New World and its people: Spain conquers, the forced labour of the mita feeds the silver mines, and in Europe Luther’s printed pamphlets split the Church.
cent.1500.powers.0.t: the largest state by population; the voyages ended in 1433
cent.1500.powers.6.t: Ivan III, then Ivan IV; Kazan taken in 1552
cent.1600.moved: Silver crosses the Pacific in the Manila galleon; the Mayflower sails in 1620; the Thirty Years' War wastes Germany 1618–1648; Galileo's telescope in 1610 and Newton's Principia in 1687.
cent.1600.art: Baroque Rome: Caravaggio, Bernini, St Peter's; the Dutch golden age of Rembrandt and Vermeer; Velázquez at Madrid; the Taj Mahal; Monteverdi at Venice; the Kano school in Edo.
cent.1600.life: The world is cold. European winters run more than a degree below the twentieth-century average, the Thames freezes for frost fairs from 1608, and in the Swiss Alps advancing glaciers crush farms and villages. The Thirty Years’ War, 1618 to 1648, leaves some regions of the Holy Roman Empire with 70 per cent fewer people. In north China drought and floods sap the Ming until rebels enter Beijing in 1644. In 1696 and 1697 famine kills a fifth of the people of Estonia and a third of Finland.
cent.1600.food: When the harvests failed, Alpine villagers ate bread of ground nutshells mixed with barley and oat flour; in England, sugar from the slave plantations of the Caribbean turned from luxury to habit, from one pound a head a year in 1670 towards twenty-five a century later.
cent.1600.smell: London in the winter of 1684, the coldest on record, smelled of the frost fair’s booths and braziers on the frozen Thames.
cent.1600.trouble: Cold, hunger and fear: as the climate worsens, wars, revolts and witch trials multiply, the accused mostly poor women and widows, blamed for late frosts, cattle plague and disease.
cent.1600.powers.1.t: Jahangir and Shah Jahan; the Taj Mahal from 1632
cent.1600.powers.3.t: silver, Flanders and the Thirty Years' War
cent.1600.powers.4.t: the VOC from 1602; the richest city of Europe
cent.1600.powers.6.t: the shogunate from 1603; the country closed
cent.1600.powers.7.t: the Romanovs from 1613; Siberia crossed to the Pacific
cent.1700.moved: Cook charts the Pacific; the First Fleet lands at Sydney in 1788; slaves cross the Atlantic in their greatest numbers; the Encyclopédie is printed 1751–1785; revolution in Philadelphia 1776 and Paris 1789.
cent.1700.art: Rococo Paris and Venice: Watteau, Tiepolo, Canaletto; Bach at Leipzig, Handel in London, Haydn and Mozart at Vienna; Rastrelli's Winter Palace 1754–1762; Hokusai's Edo prints to come.
cent.1700.life: The Atlantic slave trade reaches its height in the last two decades of the century; in all some 12.75 million Africans are loaded onto ships, held for months below deck, and up to two million die at sea. Dahomey, Oyo and Asante sell captives for guns, gunpowder, alcohol and Indian cloth. In London three children in four born in the 1730s and 1740s die before the age of five, but the cotton mills multiply: Britain spins 2.5 million pounds of raw cotton in 1750 and 52 million in 1800.
cent.1700.food: Sugar, coffee, tea and chocolate, grown by enslaved hands, become everyday pleasures in Europe; the English eat 25 pounds of sugar a head a year by 1770, up from one in 1670.
cent.1700.smell: A slave ship smelled of hundreds of captives held for months in tight, unsanitary holds, with nets rigged along the sides to catch those who jumped.
cent.1700.trouble: Freedom and its price: Britain bans its slave trade only in 1807, while the new mills set orphans and children as young as eight to work twelve to fourteen hours a day.
cent.1700.powers.0.t: Kangxi and Qianlong; the empire at its widest
cent.1700.powers.1.t: declining; Delhi sacked by Nader Shah in 1739; Plassey 1757
cent.1700.powers.2.t: Louis XIV dies in 1715; the Revolution in 1789
cent.1700.powers.3.t: union of 1707; Watt's engine; Cook's voyages from 1768
cent.1700.powers.4.t: Peter's new capital of 1703; Catherine from 1762
cent.1700.powers.5.t: Maria Theresa; the Seven Years' War
cent.1800.moved: Napoleon's armies march to Moscow and back in 1812; railways, telegraphs and steamships from the 1830s; Irish and German emigrants cross to America; the Berlin Conference of 1884–1885 partitions Africa.
cent.1800.art: Paris as the capital of painting: David, Ingres, Delacroix, then Manet, Monet and the Impressionists from 1874; Turner and Constable in London; Goya in Madrid; Beethoven and Schubert in Vienna; Hokusai and Hiroshige in Edo; the Eiffel Tower of 1889.
cent.1800.life: Steam and coal pull people into towns. Manchester’s population rises sixfold between 1771 and 1831, Bradford’s by half every ten years, London’s from under a million to three million. Newcomers crowd into slums with dirt floors and no sanitation, sewage runs raw into the rivers, and cholera kills 14,137 Londoners in 1848 and 1849. Yet the share of London children dying before five has fallen to a third. After the Great Stink of 1858, London digs 82 miles of main sewers.
cent.1800.food: Bread kept dear by the Corn Laws until 1846, chronic hunger for many until late in the century, and tea, coffee, sugar, tobacco and chocolate now within reach of ordinary Europeans.
cent.1800.smell: London in the hot summer of 1858 smelled of the Thames, thick with sewage, so badly that Parliament soaked its curtains in chloride of lime.
cent.1800.trouble: Who shares the wealth of the machines: wages rise slowly, by some estimates only 15 per cent between the 1780s and the 1850s, labourers smash threshing machines in the Swing Riots of 1830, and slavery lasts in Cuba until 1886.
cent.1800.powers.0.t: Trafalgar 1805; India, Canada, Australia; the railway from 1825
cent.1800.powers.2.t: Alexander I; the serfs freed in 1861
cent.1800.powers.6.t: Greece lost in 1830; the Crimean War 1853–1856
cent.1900.moved: Emigrants pour through Ellis Island; the Western Front freezes from the Channel to Switzerland in 1914; Lenin's train reaches Petrograd in 1917; influenza circles the world in 1918–1920.
cent.1900.art: Paris still the centre: Cézanne, Picasso and Braque's cubism from 1907, Matisse; Vienna's Secession and Klimt; the Russian avant-garde of Malevich and Kandinsky; Debussy and Stravinsky's Rite in Paris 1913; the Bauhaus at Weimar from 1919.
cent.1900.life: Two world wars bracket most lives. The first, 1914 to 1918, kills 15 to 22 million; on 1 July 1916 the British lose 19,200 dead on the Somme in one day, and four empires fall. In 1918 influenza infects 500 million, a third of humanity, and kills 25 to 50 million, 12 to 17 million of them in India. The Depression puts a quarter of Americans out of work by 1933. The second war kills 60 to 75 million, and in 1947 Partition uproots 12 to 20 million in India.
cent.1900.food: In the Depression families made do with soups, beans, noodles and the cheapest cuts, sometimes horse meat, stretching the Sunday roast into sandwiches and soup; in the 1918 epidemic some shops made customers leave their orders outside.
cent.1900.smell: The Western Front smelled of a trench line from the Channel to Switzerland, where lice, trench foot, typhus and trench fever bred in the mud.
cent.1900.trouble: Class, nation and empire: the Bolsheviks take Russia in 1917, crop prices fall by up to 60 per cent and a third of American farmers lose their land, Hitler becomes chancellor in 1933, and India and Pakistan divide in 1947.
cent.1900.powers.0.t: a quarter of the land surface; Victoria dies in 1901
cent.1900.powers.4.t: the Third Republic and its African empire
cent.1950.moved: Millions cross the new border of India and Pakistan; the Korean War begins in June 1950; Gagarin orbits in 1961; the Berlin Wall goes up in 1961; refugees and guest workers move into western Europe.
cent.1950.art: New York takes over from Paris: Pollock and Rothko; Le Corbusier's Chandigarh and Niemeyer's Brasília; Shostakovich in Leningrad; Kurosawa's Tokyo; the Sydney Opera House designed in 1957 and opened in 1973.
cent.1950.life: Polio comes back every summer: the United States records nearly 58,000 cases in 1952, and children breathe in iron lungs until Salk’s vaccine is announced in April 1955 and Sabin’s oral vaccine is licensed in 1962. Ghana wins its independence in 1957 and Algeria in 1962. In China the Great Leap Forward and its grain requisitions bring a famine, 1959 to 1961, that kills perhaps 30 to 46 million. From 1975 nearly 800,000 Vietnamese escape by boat. In 1981 American doctors first recognise AIDS.
cent.1950.food: As people move to the cities, diets shift from grains, fruit and vegetables to processed food richer in meat, sugar, refined flour and fat; in China in the famine years, people ate soil.
cent.1950.smell: A port smelled of ships’ diesel as the shipping container, invented in 1956, cut the cost of carrying goods round the world.
cent.1950.trouble: Freedom and its terms: colonies become states, pirates attack 349 of the 452 refugee boats that reach Thailand in 1981, and AIDS brings stigma as well as death.
cent.1950.powers.0.t: the dollar and the bomb; NATO from 1949
cent.1950.powers.3.t: India independent since 1947; the empire dissolving
cent.2000.moved: Container ships and the internet (the first website in 1990) tie the economies together; the Arab Spring spreads from Tunisia in 2011; COVID-19 spreads from China across the world in 2020; Russia invades Ukraine in 2022.
cent.2000.art: The art market runs through New York, London, Hong Kong and Basel; Gehry's Bilbao of 1997 and the Burj Khalifa of 2010; biennials from Venice to Sharjah; Ai Weiwei, Kiefer, Richter and Hirst in the salerooms.
cent.2000.life: In 2007, for the first time, more than half of humanity lives in cities, and by 2026 three people in four have used the internet; at any moment about half a million are in the air. Then, from Wuhan at the end of 2019, a new coronavirus: by April 2020 some 3.9 billion people, more than half the world, are under some form of lockdown, offices empty and schools close. More than 7 million deaths are confirmed, and the excess dead are put at 18 to 35 million.
cent.2000.food: City diets of processed food richer in meat, sugar, refined grains and fat, with less time to cook and more food ready-made, and body weight and cholesterol rising with income.
cent.2000.smell: An airport smelled of jet fuel and coffee, with international tourist arrivals passing a billion a year for the first time in 2012.
cent.2000.trouble: Who gets the benefits: 40.9 million people live with HIV, 32.1 million of them on treatment, 13.7 billion doses of vaccine are given against COVID-19, and the poor are often left out of what globalisation offers.
cent.2000.powers.0.t: the single superpower; the attacks of 11 September 2001
cent.2000.powers.1.t: the workshop of the world after Hong Kong's return in 1997
cent.2000.powers.2.t: the euro from 1999; Maastricht in force since 1993
cent.2000.powers.4.t: a billion people; software and services
